    Fraenkel-Mostowski atoms model variables as well as names

    Murdoch J. Gabbay1

    School of Computer Science

    Heriot-Watt University EDINBURGH EH14 4AS, Scotland murdoch.gabbay@gmail.com

    Abstract. In previous work we have shown how Fraenkel-Mostowski set theory can deliver a good model of names and their abstraction. In this paper we show that this model extends to a model of variables and their substitution, by exhibiting substitution for names in Fraenkel-Mostowski sets, as an operation on sets. Furthermore, this operation is capture-avoiding in the sense that it interacts properly with the notion of abstraction from previous work. We explore some intriguing implications of the existence of a syntax-like ‘substitution action’ on a set-theoretic universe.

    1 Introduction

    Fraenkel-Mostowski sets [5, 22] provide a model of naming and abstraction; in the case of sets representing abstract syntax these notions of name and abstraction coincide with the usual notions of ‘free name’ and ‘name-binding’ in syntax [13]. Fraenkel-Mostowski set theory can model more than syntax though; it is a foundational theory and the model of naming and abstraction which it provides, has inspired programming languages with datatypes for names and constructors to bind those names [18, 6].

    In this paper we demonstrate by a non-trivial but elementary construction on sets, that Fraenkel-Mostowski set theory is also a model of capture-avoiding substitution on names. A name with a capture-avoiding substitution action is a model of ‘a variable’, so this paper shows that the Fraenkel-Mostowski model of naming extends to a model of variables.

    We shall show that in the case of sets representing abstract syntax, the substitution action coincides with the ‘usual’ substitution deﬁned inductively on syntax. We show that on all sets — not just those representing syntax — the action satisﬁes the conditions laid out by an algebraic axiomatisation of substitution developed in previous work [12]; and we explore how one might generalise that axiomatisation to the far richer structure such as a sets universe.

    Usual notions of denotation deny variables any denotational reality; a variable in the syntax ranges over denotational elements but is not in the denotation. Put another way, ‘’ can represent any denotational element but there is no single denotational element we can point to and say ‘this represents the variable ’.

    Our construction of substitution justiﬁes a view according to which variables are denotational objects in the sets universe with equal status with other elements of the model like numbers, groups, abstract syntax, functions, and everything else that a foundational theory can express. The substitution action on the universe lets us replace these denotation objects in a sensible way.

    Map of the paper. In Section 2 we consider basic properties of FM sets (full proofs are elsewhere [13]). In Subsection 3.1 we consider what properties ‘a substitution action’ should possess, in the light of previous work. In Subsection 3.2 we consider some unsatisfactory substitution actions and use them to motivate some of the very technical aspects of our construction. In Subsection 3.3 we give the construction itself and prove its properties. In Subsection 3.4 we consider in detail one of the commutativity properties of substitution. In Section 4 we consider related work and conclusions.

    2 Fraenkel-Mostowski sets

    Fraenkel-Mostowski set theory (FM sets) is a variant of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory (ZF sets), originally introduced to prove the axiom of choice from the other axioms of ZF sets [5, 22].

    FM sets is extremely similar to ZF sets. The main difference is that in FM sets we assume a set of atoms . Atoms are ‘empty sets’ in the sense that if then . However atoms are not equal to the empty set .1 Also, an axiom insists that there be inﬁnitely many atoms.

    The reader can think of a typical FM set as being an atom, or a set containing nothing but atoms or more sets. For full details see elsewhere [10].

    3 The substitution action

    We recall our notational convention that range over distinct atoms, range over sets of atoms, lowercase range over all elements, and uppercase range over elements that are not atoms.

    3.1 The axioms

    A substitution action on FM sets is a function [] expressed in the language of FM sets (and so satisfying equivariance Theorem 2.1) taking any , an atom , and any , satisfying:

    This does not deﬁne a particular substitution on FM sets; that comes later. These are simply properties we require of the construction.

    Here by our convention range over elements of the Fraenkel-Mostowski sets universe and , , and range over distinct atoms. ranges over all functions — more on that later. [] is the Gabbay-Pitts abstraction operator — more on that later (a deﬁnition is in Deﬁnition 3.1 or previous work [13]).

    These axioms are taken from work with Mathijssen [12] in a syntax-based context (so freshness # is a notion of ‘free atoms of’ and range over terms). There it was proved that these axioms are sound and complete with respect to a closed term model where substitution is interpreted by a syntax-based ‘capture-avoiding substitution function’. Please note that we proved they are complete. So for syntax-with-binding, the axioms of substitution above capture precisely the properties of ‘capture-avoiding substitution’.2

    A model of FM sets is far larger (and richer) than any set of syntax trees. It nevertheless supports interesting and useful generalisations of the notion of ‘name’, ‘freshness’, and ‘abstraction’. Some time ago the author commented on the potential to extend this apparatus to a notion of substitution [10].

    A signiﬁcant difference between the axioms above and the axioms of [12] is that there, the ‘’ in (F) ranges over term-formers of a ﬁxed but arbitrary signature. This was appropriate in a syntactic development. Here should refer to functions on sets. But the language of FM sets can express a great many so we must read (F) carefully — more on that later. Other differences are unimportant.3

    Corollary 3.18 states that substitution is variable-like on datatypes of syntax-with-binding (that means all the usual notions of substitution on syntax). Fraenkel-Mostowski set theory can also express name-like functions. Any substitution action makes a set into a function over the atoms in its support, so that can be viewed as representing each of the functions ‘ maps to []’ for each supp(). The counterexample above shows that complex sets can become name-like. There is no conﬂict with the usual expectations for substitution; the sets concerned display structure beyond the reach of syntax.

    Let us now return to the issue of canonicity. More than one substitution action on FM sets satisﬁes Deﬁnition 3.4. Can we identify some narrower class of substitution actions of which [] is a member and [ is not? The following property generalises (abs) and has a proof similar to that of Theorem 3.13:

    Any FM set can be decomposed as a (not necessarily disjoint) union of sets of the form .4 Our substitution action is such that if then [ [] — subject to a host of sophisticated capture-avoidance issues which make up the technical meat of the deﬁnition.

    This generalises (abs), but it is a profoundly inﬁnitely property (in the decomposition, and also in the capture-avoidance conditions) and no syntax has yet been developed to express it as a neat equality between terms.

    The remarkable fact is that we obtained [] just by satisfying this one property, and it then satisﬁes all the axioms of substitution from Deﬁnition 3.4, even though those axioms all look very different.

    It is a fact that the author has developed another ‘good’ substitution action (the one outlined in this paper is the shorter and arguably the sweeter). As we mentioned above, a substitution action turns FM sets into a computational structure (of as-yet unknown power). Different substitution actions correspond to different notions of computation. A similar situation exists in the -calculus; -reduction looks simple and speciﬁc but in fact it does not pin down a single notion of computation since many strategies exist to apply it (lazy, eager, and so on). There is also freedom to include other rules, such as -reduction and -expansion, or additional constants with their own special reduction rules. -reduction qua rule is only the beginning of a larger story. The ﬁeld of logic has a similar situation; there is classical truth, intuitionistic truth, relevant truth, many-valued truth, fuzzy truth, and so on. A certain amount of core behaviour is pinned down but useful latitude also remains. It is a fact that on sets representing actual syntax, the behaviour of substitution is ﬁxed; but elsewhere latitude exists.

    It would be interesting to pin down precisely the notion of computation given by the substitution action, and in particular to discover whether it is Turing complete.

    4 Related work and Conclusions

    4.1 Related work

    CIAO Prolog [14, Extra-logical predicates] and -logic [11] include a predicate var() which is true of when is a variable symbol (its use is to guide proof-search). The functional programming language CURRY [15] has similar constructs. These ‘non-standard’ functions behave like that are not variable-like, and so current denotational methods ﬁnd them hard to account for.

    Fine [9] has undertaken a philosophical axiomatic investigation of dependency between objects. A connection may be established if we take substitution to give a notion of ‘correlation’ between sets; for example if [, or [[], then and are ‘correlated’.

    Aczel’s ‘generalised set theory’ [2] and ‘universes with parameters’ [3] model variable symbols (Aczel calls them parameters) as atoms in a ZFA-like set theory. The resemblance ends there; we discover structure inherent in a known and relatively simple set theory, whereas Aczel imposes all the structure he needs as extra axioms on names. Aczel’s programme is also different and concerns itself with coinductive structures and non-wellfounded set theory [1] as a semantics for behaviour. Aczel’s substitution action is not capture-avoiding, in the sense that [[] always, like the naïve substitution action [ from Subsection 3.2. .

    Nominal terms [23] come equipped with a substitution action, but this is for context variables and is not capture-avoiding. A capture-avoiding substitution action has been axiomatised using equalities between nominal terms [12]; our Theorem 3.14 can be read as stating that the construction in this paper validates those axioms (but it is not built out of syntax).

    Other axioms for substitution exist; for example in work by Salibra [19], by Beeson [4], by Crabbé [7], and by Feldmann [8]. The axioms of Crabbé and Feldmann are not of capture-avoiding substitution. The axioms of Salibra and Beeson are. Salibra is interested in models but his models are abstract (he does universal algebra). Beeson is interested in theorem-proving. The axioms of Salibra and Beeson for substitution are embedded in larger theories of Turing-complete computation based on the -calculus, which gives their treatment a very different ﬂavour from ours. Feldman’s axioms are based on a concrete model using environments (functions mapping variables to denotational objects) which is very different from our model which is based on a set-theory (a far larger construction) and in which variables inhabit the denotation in a more direct sense.

    Schmidt-Schauß and Siekmann introduce uniﬁcation algebra [20] and Williams introduces instantiation theory [24]. In both cases an axiomatic approach is taken to substitution. The idea is to free the theory of uniﬁcation from (the shackles of) syntax and give an axiomatic account of instantiation and uniﬁcation. The axioms phrase abstract versions of instantiation and uniﬁcation as known in syntax; in this paper we have presented a concrete model of an entirely independent structure (the axioms of set theory) which is also a model of substitution.

    The work by Schmidt-Schauß, Siekmann, and Williams, all involve ‘bespoke’ (axiomatic) semantics which build in the basic elements of the object of study. Aczel’s set theories [2, 3] also contain elements clearly identiﬁable as variables along with dedicated axioms clearly tailor-made to endow them with substitution. Abstraction and capture-avoidance, where these are considered at all, are always ‘bespoke’.

    4.2 Conclusions

    In this paper we have discovered a capture-avoiding substitution action, deﬁned purely by -induction on set structure, and hiding in a set theory known for the better part of a century [5, 22]. This raises philosophical questions about substitution, so familiar as a concrete operation on syntax.

    The FM model displays substitution behaviour spontaneously and not because of any obvious design to ‘make it work’; the axioms of FM sets have no evident features to suggest the application we have made of it in this paper. Indeed the theory was designed with a quite different application in mind, and even after the author and Pitts re-discovered it and applied it to syntax-with-binding [13], the substitution action remained hidden for several years.

    The existence of universes of sets with a substitution action raises some interesting prospects.

    FM sets contains sets representing syntax and sets representing semantics and the set theory marks no barrier between them. Substitution extends smoothly from sets representing syntax to all sets. Can we extend syntax-based proof-methods along this substitution action to denotation; for example by using -induction principles on sets of denotations with their substitution action, like we use inductive arguments on syntax? Can we use FM sets as an arena to consider the ‘non-standard’ calculi and logics mentioned in the Related Work? Is it possible to now consider FM semantics for well-understood systems such as name-passing calculi [17]?

    We should try to understand the computational content of the substitution action; a set can be considered a function over the atoms in its support, with ‘ applied to ’ interpreted as [] (we get a different function for each supp()). What is the precise power of this notion of computation; is it Turing complete?

    If we have a sets universe with a substitution action we can consider all the things that are usually done with syntax (and arguably trapped in syntax) but now we can give them a more abstract meaning; for example we can consider uniﬁcation, matching, rewriting, and to some extent solutions to simultaneous equations — on Fraenkel-Mostowski sets. This raises the intriguing possibility that giving a set-theoretic semantics for example to rewriting systems may have a similar signiﬁcance as Scott’s set-theoretic semantics of the -calculus [21].

    We hope this work will stimulate a different view of variables in syntax and semantics and open new possibilities in both.
